**Evaluating user request**

I see the user has provided a few keywords, but it's a bit ambiguous. I think it’s best to offer a concise overview of UK development finance and lending trends, particularly related to property development finance. I should mention that if they were referring to development finance institutions (DFIs), it might help to clarify that. Also, I’ll need to ensure I include dates and cite all factual statements from reliable internet sources. Let’s get started!

If by **“development finance”** you mean **UK property development lending** (the usual market meaning), the current picture is:

- **Credit availability has improved since 2024**, especially for the **commercial real estate / development-related** segment. In the Bank of England’s **2025 Q4 Credit Conditions Survey**, lenders reported a **positive net balance for credit availability to the commercial real estate sector** in both the prior three months and the next three months, suggesting supply was still expanding rather than contracting. ([bankofengland.co.uk](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/credit-conditions-survey/2025/2025-q4?utm_source=openai))
- That said, **demand is not especially strong**. Bank of England business contacts said in **July 2026** that clients were still delaying decisions, reducing activity in **commercial real estate deals**, while in **June 2026** the Bank said access to finance remained **uneven for smaller firms**. ([bankofengland.co.uk](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/agents-summary/2026/july-2026?utm_source=openai))
- **Construction/development activity itself remains soft.** The Bank’s **December 2025** agents’ summary said **new housebuilding and commercial projects were below the prior year** because of **high build and funding costs**. ([bankofengland.co.uk](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/agents-summary/2025/december-2025?utm_source=openai))
- A key trend is a **more selective lending market**: larger, stronger borrowers can still access bank and private credit more easily, while **SMEs and construction-linked borrowers** face a tougher environment. The Bank of England noted in **July 2026** there was **less appetite to lend to small and medium-sized firms and the construction sector**. ([bankofengland.co.uk](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/agents-summary/2026/july-2026?utm_source=openai))
- There is also evidence that **competition among lenders increased during 2025**, with lenders citing **market share objectives** as a factor supporting commercial real estate credit availability. ([bankofengland.co.uk](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/credit-conditions-survey/2025/2025-q4?utm_source=openai))
- For **SME housebuilders**, policy support has remained important. The British Business Bank says its **ENABLE Build** programme is designed to **increase the availability of finance to UK SME house builders**, and by **3 June 2025** the Bank said its structured guarantee programmes, including ENABLE Build, had delivered **£5bn of lending** in total. ([british-business-bank.co.uk](https://www.british-business-bank.co.uk/finance-options/debt-finance/enable-programmes/enable-build?utm_source=openai))
- Another structural trend is **funding diversification**. The British Business Bank says fintech and alternative lenders have become a growing source of UK business and property-related finance, with **annual origination volumes above £2bn** across several specialist lending categories. ([british-business-bank.co.uk](https://www.british-business-bank.co.uk/finance-options/debt-finance/fintech?utm_source=openai))

**In plain English:**  
The UK development finance market looks **more open than it was at the tightest point of the rate shock**, but it is still **cautious, expensive, and highly selective**. Better-quality schemes and experienced sponsors can get funded; weaker schemes, smaller developers, and marginal projects are still finding the market difficult. ([bankofengland.co.uk](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/credit-conditions-survey/2025/2025-q4?utm_source=openai))
